final_proof:
Work in ZF, without any form of the axiom of choice, and write ω for the set of natural numbers. We use the well-order collapse fact: every well-ordered set (A,R) is isomorphic to a unique ordinal, called its order type. This fact requires no choice. Indeed, well-founded recursion defines p(a)={p(b):b R a}. Well-founded induction on R shows simultaneously that each p(a) is an ordinal and that p(b)∈p(a) if and only if b R a. Thus p is an order isomorphism from (A,R) onto its range, and its range is a transitive set of ordinals, hence an ordinal. Uniqueness follows by induction, since an isomorphism between two ordinals must fix every element.

Let S be the set of all pairs (A,R) such that A is a subset of ω and R is a well-ordering of A. This is a set, since it can be obtained by Separation from P(ω)×P(ω×ω). By Replacement, the collection

H={ot(A,R):(A,R) in S}

of the order types of all well-ordered subsets of ω is also a set. Every member of H is an ordinal. Moreover, H is transitive. To see this, suppose α is in H and β is in α. Choose (A,R) in S and an order isomorphism e:(A,R)→(α,∈). If a is the unique element of A with e(a)=β, then the R-initial segment A_a={x in A:x R a}, with R restricted to it, is a well-ordering of a subset of ω, and e restricts to an isomorphism from A_a onto β. Hence β is in H. Thus H is a transitive set all of whose elements are ordinals, so H itself is an ordinal. Put Ω=H and give it its usual membership well-order.

There is no injection from Ω into ω. For suppose that f:Ω→ω were injective. Its image A=f[Ω] is a subset of ω. Transfer the membership order on Ω to A by declaring f(ξ) R f(η) exactly when ξ∈η. Then (A,R) is a well-ordered subset of ω of order type Ω. By the definition of H, this would give Ω∈H. Since H=Ω, it would follow that Ω∈Ω, which is impossible for an ordinal. Therefore Ω does not inject into ω, and in particular Ω is uncountable. (Also, ω∈H, using the usual well-order of ω, so Ω is certainly infinite.)

It remains to check the required property. Let I be any proper initial segment of Ω. Because Ω is well-ordered, the complement Ω\I has a least element α, and downward closure of I gives I={ξ∈Ω:ξ∈α}=α. In particular, α∈Ω=H. Consequently there is a subset A of ω with a well-ordering whose order type is α. An isomorphism with that well-order, followed by the inclusion A⊆ω, gives an injection of α (and hence of I) into ω. Thus I is countable in the sense of being at most countable. If 'countable' is instead defined to mean finite or equipotent with ω, the same conclusion follows: a finite α is finite, while an infinite ordinal α contains ω; together with the injection α→ω, the Cantor–Bernstein theorem yields a bijection α≅ω. Cantor–Bernstein is provable in ZF.

Hence Ω is an uncountable well-ordered set every proper initial segment of which is countable. This also explains the word 'minimal': if an uncountable well-ordered set has order type γ, then γ cannot be less than Ω, since every ordinal below Ω is countable; by comparability of ordinals, Ω≤γ. No choice principle was used.
